fixes.explanation: That's the royal law, baker. James says, "If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing well." (James 2:8) It comes from Leviticus 19:18, and it fits this whole scene. Giving someone the standing spot isn't exactly loving them like yourself.

That's the one, friend. James opens with it: "My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism." (James 2:1) He puts the instruction right alongside holding out their faith in Jesus. Short sentence, big weight.

Gossip is a real problem, but James isn't talking about it here. His words are "…do not show favoritism." (James 2:1) Favoritism means treating people differently because of who they are. I've seen a version of it at a cookie table, friend, when somebody's eyeing the biggest cookie in the batch.

Right on the money. James says the man in fine clothes gets, "Here is a seat of honor…" (James 2:3) The best seat, handed over because of the fine clothes. Meanwhile the poor man hears something very different.

Nice guess, but no tree in this one. James has the man in fine clothes told, "Here is a seat of honor…" (James 2:3) The scene is a meeting, and the seating is the whole problem. The man with the gold ring gets the honored seat, and the poor man hears something very different.

That's right, baker. James says the poor man hears, "You must stand…" or "Sit at my feet…" (James 2:3) So he gets standing or the spot at somebody's feet. The man in fine clothes gets the seat of honor, and that's exactly the favoritism James is calling out.

Judges is the word, friend. James says they've "…become judges with evil thoughts?" (James 2:4) Nobody handed them a gavel, but sorting people by their clothes is judging all the same. I think that's the sting of it.

You got it, baker. James asks, "Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?" (James 2:6) He's just shown them the picture of the man with the gold ring getting the seat of honor. Now he asks them to think about who the rich are to them.
The Romans are not named here, friend. James asks, "Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?" (James 2:6) The text puts the rich in the spotlight. That's who he points to.

No priests in this verse, friend. James says, "Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?" (James 2:6) The text puts the rich in the spotlight. He asks it as a question, and the answer is right there in the verse.

The Sabbath doesn't come up in this passage, friend. James says, "…judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful." (James 2:13) The test he gives is mercy. That fits everything he's said about the poor man told to stand or sit at someone's feet.

Mercy, baker! James ends with, "Mercy triumphs over judgment." (James 2:13) After all that talk about law and sin, that last line is a good one to land on. It follows right after the line about those who haven't been merciful.

Wisdom is a good word, friend, and James brings it up in James 1:5. But here he ends with, "Mercy triumphs over judgment." (James 2:13) It's the very thing the favoritism was missing. Mercy gets the last word.
